Many scenarios for the energy transition consider green ammonia. The technologically most mature production process combines water electrolysis and Haber-Bosch process (EHB). Its costs are dominated by electrolyzer investment costs and electricity. Emerging pathways researched in academia, start-ups, and industry try to reduce costs by changing sub-processes and chemistry. However, it remains unclear which pathways have the potential to outperform EHB, if any. We assess relevant emerging pathways, compare to EHB in terms of costs and energy demand, and derive performance targets. Many pathways investigated in the literature, such as metalmediated electrolysis, have theoretical minimal energy demands well above the actual energy demand of EHB; consequently, they cannot produce ammonia at competitive costs due to the high influence of electricity costs. Any novel pathway must employ simple and energy-effective chemistry to substantially reduce costs. Identified performance targets are applicable to novel pathways and can guide research, industry, and policy makers.

Abstract Rare-earth engineering of CeO2 offers a route to enhance Ru-based catalysts for ammonia synthesis by tailoring oxygen vacancies and metal–support interactions. Herein, we systematically synthesized and benchmarked Ru catalysts supported on RE (=Gd, La, and Sm)-modified CeO2 under identical conditions to establish promoter-structure–activity relationships. Rare-earth incorporation increased the Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio, oxygen-vacancy concentration, and weak acidic sites, facilitating electron transfer to Ru, promoting N2 activation, and potentially facilitating interfacial hydrogen spillover. H2-TPD suggested improved hydrogen mobility and utilization at the Ru/CeO2 interface. Ru/GdCeO exhibited the highest NH3 synthesis rate of (19.80 ± 0.98) mmol g–1h–1 at 400 °C and 1.5 MPa, with an N2:H2 ratio of 1:2 and WHSV = 13,500 mL g–1 h–1, yielding 3.53 vol % NH3 in the reactor effluent. Such superior performance may be associated with optimized Ru-support interactions and abundant oxygen vacancies. These findings establish Gd as the most effective promoter for Ru/CeO2 under mild synthesis conditions.

Abstract Ammonia, an emerging energy carrier, demands advanced catalysts for synthesis under mild conditions to integrate with green hydrogen. We herein establish a family of metal fluoride supports (MFn, M = Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, or Ba) as a tunable “all-in-one” platform for ruthenium (Ru) catalysts. These Ru/MFn systems unify the critical merits of various existing catalysts, such as support-mediated activation of reactants and air stability. Varying the host cation can direct the catalytic pathway. Consequently, Ru/NaF exhibits excellent turnover frequency, while Ru/BaF2 delivers an NH3 synthesis rate of 58.0 mmolNH3 gcat–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 0.9 MPa─surpassing all reported Ru-based catalysts with ≤4 wt % Ru and without external promoters. Advanced characterization reveals that the fluorine vacancy formation energies of the alkali and alkaline-earth lattices, together with the vacancy-reactant interactions, dictate the divergent catalytic mechanisms mediated by different active sites. This work expands the chemistry of metal fluorides, launching a new paradigm for potentially viable NH3-synthesis under mild conditions.
